title: Main thread, input and frame mechanics
scopeHtml: Scope: what runs on the main thread, the frame deadline, vsync/Choreographer, input dispatch and its 5 s timeout, StrictMode, AsyncTask replacement, threading options, touch dispatch, SurfaceView vs TextureView. Looper internals are in the M1 chunk and profiling playbooks belong to A6.

questions.subtopic: What runs on the main thread
questions.promptHtml: What exactly runs on an Android app's main (UI) thread, and what are you not allowed to do there?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Every jank and ANR bug starts with someone doing the wrong work on this thread. They want to see if you know the list is wider than "UI code".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The main thread is the one thread that runs the app's Looper. Lifecycle callbacks of Activity, Service, BroadcastReceiver and Application, input event handling, measure/layout/draw of the view tree, and anything posted via Handler or Dispatchers.Main all run there serially. Views can only be touched from it. So anything slow, like disk, network or heavy computation, blocks input and frames and eventually causes an ANR.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The process entry point is ActivityThread.main(). It calls Looper.prepareMainLooper(), attaches to system_server, then Looper.loop() forever. Every callback from the system arrives as a Message on that queue, executed one at a time, run-to-completion.

Main thread Looper (one queue, one consumer)
 ├─ Activity/Fragment lifecycle (onCreate ... onDestroy)
 ├─ Service callbacks (onCreate, onStartCommand, onBind, onDestroy)
 ├─ BroadcastReceiver.onReceive
 ├─ Application.onCreate, ContentProvider.onCreate
 ├─ Input event handling (onTouchEvent, onClick, onKey)
 ├─ Choreographer frame callbacks: animation, measure/layout, record draw
 └─ Handler.post / View.post / Dispatchers.Main / LiveData observers

What is NOT on the main thread: ContentProvider query/insert (they run on Binder threads), Binder calls received by your own bound service (Binder pool, up to 16 threads by default), and the actual GPU draw (RenderThread, API 21+). Outgoing Binder calls made from the main thread block the main thread until the remote answers, which is the hidden cost behind many ANRs.

Forbidden or harmful on main: network (throws NetworkOnMainThreadException for apps targeting API 11+), disk I/O (SharedPreferences first load, SQLite, file reads), JSON parsing of big payloads, bitmap decoding, locks held by other threads, synchronous Binder calls to slow services, Thread.sleep.

The thread is single, so one 300 ms operation delays everything behind it, including input already queued.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken: blocks main for the full disk+parse time
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    val json = File(filesDir, "catalog.json").readText()   // disk I/O on main
    adapter.submit(parse(json))                           // CPU on main
}

// Better
lifecycleScope.launch {
    val items = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { parse(File(filesDir, "catalog.json").readText()) }
    adapter.submit(items)   // back on Main
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing "main thread = UI only". BroadcastReceiver.onReceive and Service.onStartCommand are on main too.
  • Thinking lifecycleScope.launch {} leaves main. It starts on Dispatchers.Main.immediate; blocking code inside still blocks.
  • Assuming ContentProvider queries are on main (they are on Binder threads; only onCreate is on main).
  • Moving work to a thread and then join()/get()-ing on main, which is the same block.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is a single UI thread designed that way? → View hierarchy is not thread-safe; locking every setter would be slow and deadlock-prone, so a single-threaded model with message passing is used.
  2. Is it OK to read a small SharedPreferences value on main? → First access loads the whole XML from disk; later reads are memory. Still a risk on cold start and at apply() time (see StrictMode question).
  3. How do you throw an error if a method must not run on main? → Looper.getMainLooper().isCurrentThread (API 23+) or @WorkerThread plus lint; at runtime check(Looper.myLooper() != Looper.getMainLooper()).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "UI work only, do network on a background thread." Senior: enumerates all components that run there, knows ContentProvider and Binder-received calls run elsewhere, treats outgoing Binder calls as main-thread blocking, and frames the rule as a time budget per message, not a list of banned APIs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team's ANR cluster traced to PackageManager.getInstalledApplications() called in a receiver on a loaded device; it is a Binder call, so it looked "cheap" in code review.

questions.promptHtml: What is the frame deadline on Android, and how does it change on 90/120 Hz devices? What happens when you miss it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you reason about jank in milliseconds and know the deadline is not a constant 16 ms.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The deadline is 1000 ms divided by the display refresh rate: 16.67 ms at 60 Hz, 11.1 ms at 90 Hz, 8.33 ms at 120 Hz. In that window the main thread must run input, animation, measure/layout and record draw, and the RenderThread must finish GPU work. If it misses vsync, the previous frame is shown again, so the user sees a dropped frame as jank.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Math: 1000/60 = 16.67 ms; 1000/90 = 11.11 ms; 1000/120 = 8.33 ms; 1000/144 = 6.94 ms.

The budget is not all yours. SurfaceFlinger composition and the RenderThread take part of it, so a practical main-thread budget at 60 Hz is closer to 8-10 ms of work to be safe, and about 4-5 ms at 120 Hz.

vsync N                     vsync N+1                   vsync N+2
 |--- UI thread work ---|     |--- present frame N --->
      |-- RenderThread --|
 If UI thread + RenderThread > 1 period: frame N is not ready at N+1,
 screen re-shows frame N-1 (dropped frame), next frame is also late (pipeline latency).

Since API 21 drawing is split: UI thread builds display lists (RecordingCanvas), then syncAndDrawFrame hands them to RenderThread which issues GL/Vulkan commands. Buffers go through a BufferQueue to SurfaceFlinger, which composites at vsync. Triple buffering lets the UI thread start the next frame while one is being scanned out, trading one frame of latency for throughput.

Variable refresh rate: the device may run 60/90/120 depending on content and apps can hint with Surface.setFrameRate / View.setRequestedFrameRate (newer releases), so never hardcode 16 ms. Read display.refreshRate or use frame timestamps from Choreographer.

When missed: logcat shows Choreographer: Skipped N frames! The application may be doing too much work on its main thread if N >= 30 (a threshold in Choreographer source). Smaller misses show only in FrameMetrics/Perfetto.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val rate = display?.refreshRate ?: 60f            // Context with a display (Activity)
val frameBudgetMs = 1000f / rate                  // 8.33 on a 120 Hz panel

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Hardcoding 16 ms thresholds in perf tests; they pass on 60 Hz and hide jank on 120 Hz.
  • Counting only main-thread time; RenderThread bound frames (big blur, overdraw) miss deadlines with an idle main thread.
  • Measuring on an emulator or debug build, where results are not representative.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Do all devices at 120 Hz render at 120 fps? → No. Many panels adapt (LTPO or content-based); static content drops to low rates, scrolling goes high.
  2. What is the "Skipped frames" message threshold? → 30 frames in Choreographer; absent message does not mean smooth.
  3. Why does one slow frame cause two bad frames? → The pipeline is already one buffer behind; the next frame starts late and inherits the delay unless the app catches up.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "16 ms or you drop frames." Senior: computes the budget per refresh rate, splits it between UI thread, RenderThread and SurfaceFlinger, and designs tests relative to the device's actual rate.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An animation tuned on a 60 Hz test phone stuttered on newly shipped 120 Hz flagships because per-frame work that fit in 16 ms did not fit in 8.3 ms.

questions.promptHtml: Explain how a vsync signal turns into a drawn frame in the View system. What is the order of Choreographer callbacks?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand why invalidate() does not draw immediately and why animation and layout order matters.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: SurfaceFlinger sends vsync to the app via DisplayEventReceiver. Choreographer, on the main thread, runs callbacks in a fixed order for that frame: input, animation, insets animation, traversal (measure/layout/draw record), and commit. invalidate() or requestLayout() only schedules a traversal for the next vsync, so many calls in one frame coalesce into a single draw.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism:

  1. A view calls requestLayout()/invalidate(). It propagates up to ViewRootImpl.scheduleTraversals().
  2. scheduleTraversals posts a sync barrier on the main MessageQueue (so ordinary messages cannot delay the traversal), then Choreographer.postCallback(CALLBACK_TRAVERSAL, ...).
  3. Choreographer requests the next vsync from DisplayEventReceiver.
  4. On vsync, FrameDisplayEventReceiver posts an asynchronous message (it passes the barrier) that runs doFrame().
  5. doFrame runs, in order: CALLBACK_INPUT, CALLBACK_ANIMATION, CALLBACK_INSETS_ANIMATION (API 30+), CALLBACK_TRAVERSAL, CALLBACK_COMMIT.
  6. In traversal: doTraversal removes the barrier, then performTraversals does measure, layout, then draw, which records a display list and syncs to RenderThread.
vsync ──> doFrame(frameTimeNanos)
            1 INPUT      batched MotionEvents delivered here
            2 ANIMATION  ValueAnimator / ObjectAnimator ticks (AnimationHandler)
            3 INSETS_ANIMATION
            4 TRAVERSAL  measure -> layout -> draw(record) -> sync to RenderThread
            5 COMMIT     fix up frame time after long frames

Consequences: animators set values before layout, so the same frame renders the new values. Modifying state in onDraw that triggers invalidate() loops once per frame. Touch events are batched and delivered at the input stage, so touch latency is up to one frame.

Choreographer.getInstance().postFrameCallback { frameTimeNanos -> } runs in the animation stage and gives you the vsync timestamp; use it for time-based custom animations. Jetpack Compose uses the same Choreographer (via MonotonicFrameClock) as its frame source.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class FpsProbe : Choreographer.FrameCallback {
    private var last = 0L
    override fun doFrame(frameTimeNanos: Long) {
        if (last != 0L) {
            val dtMs = (frameTimeNanos - last) / 1_000_000.0
            if (dtMs > 20) Log.w("Jank", "frame gap %.1f ms".format(dtMs))
        }
        last = frameTimeNanos
        Choreographer.getInstance().postFrameCallback(this)   // must re-post each frame
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting to re-post postFrameCallback; it fires once.
  • Using System.currentTimeMillis() for animation progress instead of frameTimeNanos.
  • Believing invalidate() draws synchronously; it only marks dirty and schedules.
  • Doing heavy work in a frame callback; it runs inside the same frame budget.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why a sync barrier? → So queued ordinary messages (e.g., a 50 ms task) cannot starve the traversal that is waiting for vsync; async messages bypass it. (Barrier internals: M1 chunk.)
  2. What if the main thread is busy when vsync arrives? → doFrame runs late; Choreographer computes the skipped frames and logs when >= 30; animators jump by elapsed time.
  3. Does View.post run before or after the traversal? → Before attach, it is queued and executed after the first traversal; after attach it is a normal Handler message, so it can run before or after the next frame depending on queue order.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Choreographer syncs drawing to vsync." Senior: gives the callback order, the barrier mechanism, explains invalidation coalescing, and uses it to explain why animation values never tear against layout.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A custom progress view re-posted invalidate() from onDraw plus a handler loop, doubling work per frame; moving to one postFrameCallback halved CPU on low-end devices.

questions.promptHtml: Since Android 5 there is a RenderThread. What does it do, and what does it change about where jank can come from?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who only know "don't block main" from those who can reason about GPU-bound or sync-bound frames.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The UI thread records drawing commands into display lists, then hands them to the RenderThread, which replays them on the GPU. So main thread work and GPU work are pipelined. Jank can now come from either: slow measure/layout/record on main, or heavy GPU work like overdraw, blur or big bitmap uploads on RenderThread. Some operations, like RenderNode property animations, can run on RenderThread even when main is busy.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Flow per frame (hardware-accelerated, default since API 14 for targetSdk 14+):

UI thread:  input -> animate -> measure -> layout -> draw() records RenderNodes
              |
              +-- syncAndDrawFrame: copies dirty display-list state (short blocking sync)
RenderThread:  replays display lists -> GL/Vulkan (Skia) -> swapBuffers -> BufferQueue
SurfaceFlinger: composes layers at next vsync

The sync step blocks the UI thread briefly: RenderThread must copy updated properties and upload new bitmaps/textures to GPU memory. Large bitmap first draws therefore show up as a long "sync/upload" slice on the UI thread (Perfetto: Texture upload, syncFrameState).

Animation of View.alpha, translationX/Y, scaleX/Y, rotation on a hardware layer can be run by RenderNodeAnimator / ViewPropertyAnimator on RenderThread when the animator is a simple property animation with no listeners requiring main; this is why such animations can stay smooth while main is busy. Animating layout_width or text size always needs main-thread measure/layout.

Where each cost lands:

Symptom Usual cause
Long Choreographer#doFrame / traversal on main deep hierarchy, nested weights, onDraw allocation
Long RenderThread DrawFrame overdraw, blur, saveLayer, big clip paths, complex shaders
Long texture upload at first draw huge bitmap decoded on main and drawn first time
Fine CPU, still janky GPU or SurfaceFlinger bound, thermal throttling

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Cheap on RenderThread: property animation, no relayout
view.animate().translationY(0f).alpha(1f).setDuration(200).start()

// Costly: forces layout every frame on main
ValueAnimator.ofInt(0, 500).apply {
    addUpdateListener { view.layoutParams.height = it.animatedValue as Int; view.requestLayout() }
}.start()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Profiling only the main thread and declaring "no jank" while RenderThread overruns.
  • Animating layout params instead of transforms.
  • Decoding a 4000x3000 bitmap and drawing it into a 100 dp view (upload cost scales with source size).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What are hardware layers (setLayerType(LAYER_TYPE_HARDWARE)) good for? → Cache a view as a GPU texture for transform/alpha animations; costs GPU memory and a re-render when invalidated, so enable only during the animation.
  2. Is software rendering still a thing? → Only when hardwareAccelerated=false or some canvas ops unsupported; slow and rare.
  3. How would you tell main-bound from GPU-bound in a trace? → Compare doFrame slice length versus DrawFrame on RenderThread and GPU completion in Perfetto frame timeline (tooling detail is A6).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Keep onDraw fast." Senior: describes the two-thread pipeline, the blocking sync point, which animations bypass main, and chooses transforms and layers deliberately.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feed card with a 12 MP header image and a blur overlay was smooth on main in the profiler yet dropped to 30 fps on mid-range GPUs; downsampling and removing the blur fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: Walk through how a touch event travels through the View hierarchy. What do dispatchTouchEvent, onInterceptTouchEvent and onTouchEvent each do, and what do their return values mean?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Gesture conflicts (scroll in scroll, swipe in pager) are common bugs; you need the mechanism to fix them.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The event goes Activity.dispatchTouchEvent, then the window and DecorView, then down ViewGroups via dispatchTouchEvent. Each ViewGroup may steal the gesture in onInterceptTouchEvent. The deepest view that returns true from onTouchEvent on ACTION_DOWN becomes the touch target and receives the rest of the gesture. If a parent intercepts later, the child gets ACTION_CANCEL.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Activity.dispatchTouchEvent
  -> Window -> DecorView.dispatchTouchEvent
     -> ViewGroup A.dispatchTouchEvent
          onInterceptTouchEvent? (true => A handles via its own onTouchEvent)
          -> ViewGroup B ... -> View.dispatchTouchEvent
                 OnTouchListener.onTouch (if set) -> if true, onTouchEvent skipped
                 onTouchEvent -> performClick on ACTION_UP
  unhandled => bubbles back up: B.onTouchEvent, A.onTouchEvent, Activity.onTouchEvent

Rules:

  • On ACTION_DOWN, ViewGroup clears the previous touch target and checks onInterceptTouchEvent (unless FLAG_DISALLOW_INTERCEPT set; this flag is reset on every DOWN).
  • If no child consumes DOWN (returns false), the ViewGroup itself becomes the handler (calls its own onTouchEvent); subsequent events of this gesture do not reach the children.
  • A child that consumed DOWN gets MOVE/UP directly; the parent still calls onInterceptTouchEvent for each event. If it returns true, the child receives one ACTION_CANCEL and later events go to the parent.
  • requestDisallowInterceptTouchEvent(true) from a child stops ancestors from intercepting for the rest of the gesture.
  • onInterceptTouchEvent only exists on ViewGroup. OnTouchListener runs before onTouchEvent; onClick fires from onTouchEvent's ACTION_UP, so returning true from an OnTouchListener on ACTION_UP suppresses the click.

Modern scrolling uses nested scrolling (NestedScrollingParent3/Child3), which avoids most manual intercept code. All of this runs on the main thread inside the Choreographer input stage.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class HorizontalGuard(ctx: Context) : FrameLayout(ctx) {
    private var downX = 0f; private var downY = 0f
    override fun onInterceptTouchEvent(e: MotionEvent): Boolean {
        when (e.actionMasked) {
            MotionEvent.ACTION_DOWN -> { downX = e.x; downY = e.y }
            MotionEvent.ACTION_MOVE -> {
                val dx = kotlin.math.abs(e.x - downX); val dy = kotlin.math.abs(e.y - downY)
                val slop = ViewConfiguration.get(context).scaledTouchSlop
                if (dx > slop && dx > dy) return true   // we take horizontal drags
            }
        }
        return false   // never intercept DOWN, or children can't be targets
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Returning true from onInterceptTouchEvent on DOWN: the child never receives the gesture.
  • Returning false from onTouchEvent on DOWN and expecting MOVE events.
  • Forgetting performClick() for accessibility in custom onTouchEvent.
  • Calling requestDisallowInterceptTouchEvent without resetting on CANCEL/UP (it resets automatically on next DOWN).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does the child get ACTION_CANCEL? → So it can reset its pressed/drag state once the parent takes over.
  2. How does multi-touch change it? → ACTION_POINTER_DOWN/UP carry actionIndex; use actionMasked and pointer ids, not indexes, across events.
  3. Where does Compose differ? → Pointer input uses its own hit test and propagation passes (Initial, Main, Final) and interop via AndroidView; deeper detail is in A3.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: lists the three methods. Senior: explains target selection on DOWN, the CANCEL contract, FLAG_DISALLOW_INTERCEPT, and prefers nested scrolling over manual intercept.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A horizontal carousel inside a bottom sheet and a vertical RecyclerView fought over gestures, producing sticky scroll until the carousel called requestDisallowInterceptTouchEvent on horizontal slop.

questions.promptHtml: AsyncTask is deprecated. What was wrong with it and what replaces it today?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Legacy codebases still contain it; migrating needs knowledge of its quirks.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: AsyncTask was deprecated in API 30 (Android 11). It leaked Activities via inner classes, did not survive configuration changes, had a serial executor by default that made tasks queue behind one another, and swallowed cancel semantics. Today I use Kotlin coroutines with structured concurrency tied to a lifecycle scope, or an Executor for Java, and WorkManager when the work must survive the process.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Behavior history: pre-Donut serial, Donut-Gingerbread parallel pool, Honeycomb (API 11) onward default SERIAL_EXECUTOR for apps targeting 13+. executeOnExecutor(THREAD_POOL_EXECUTOR) gave parallelism but a bounded pool (core = CPU+1, max 2*CPU+1, queue 128), so 128+ queued tasks throw RejectedExecutionException.

Problems:

Problem Effect
Non-static inner class holds Activity, leak until task ends
onPostExecute after destroy touches dead views or crashes
No lifecycle binding rotation restarts or orphans work
Serial queue one slow task blocks all
Exceptions uncaught exception in doInBackground crashes the process

AsyncTask is deprecated, not removed from the framework as of API 36; old binaries still run. AndroidX had a compat alternative in the past, not recommended.

Replacements:

Need Use
Work tied to a screen viewModelScope/lifecycleScope + withContext(Dispatchers.IO)
Java codebase, fire and forget Executors.newFixedThreadPool + Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())
Must finish even if app closes WorkManager (A5), or foreground service for user-visible
Streams of results Flow

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Before
class LoadTask : AsyncTask<Void, Void, List<Item>>() {
    override fun doInBackground(vararg p: Void?) = repo.loadBlocking()
    override fun onPostExecute(r: List<Item>) { adapter.submit(r) }   // may run after destroy
}
// After
viewModelScope.launch {
    val items = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { repo.loadBlocking() }
    _state.value = items
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Replacing with a raw Thread and no cancellation: same leaks, less structure.
  • Using GlobalScope: same orphaning problem as AsyncTask.
  • Catching CancellationException in a generic catch (e: Exception) and breaking cancellation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you map publishProgress? → Emit via Flow/StateFlow or withContext(Main) updates.
  2. How do you map cancel(true)? → Job.cancel; blocking code must be cooperative (ensureActive, runInterruptible).
  3. What if the legacy code is Java with 200 AsyncTasks? → Wrap via a small executor-based helper first, then migrate screen by screen (see the migration scenario in this chunk).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Use coroutines." Senior: lists exact failure modes, knows the executor pool bounds, picks the replacement per durability need, and plans an incremental migration.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: RejectedExecutionException crashes at 128 queued tasks appeared when a screen enqueued an AsyncTask per RecyclerView row on fling.

questions.promptHtml: Give an overview of threading options on Android and how you choose between them.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows whether you have a decision framework rather than a favorite tool.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I choose by lifetime and need. Coroutines with a lifecycle-bound scope for work tied to UI; Executors or dispatchers for pooled blocking work; HandlerThread when I need a single looper thread with ordered messages; WorkManager for guaranteed deferrable work; foreground service for user-visible long running work. Raw Thread I avoid except in libraries.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Option Thread model Lifecycle aware Survives process death Best for
Coroutines Dispatchers.IO/Default/Main shared pools yes via scope no most app work
Executor / ThreadPoolExecutor you size the pool no no Java code, libs
HandlerThread one looper thread, message queue no no ordered serial tasks, sensors, camera callbacks
Thread one OS thread no no rare, one-off
RxJava Schedulers pools via disposables no legacy reactive codebases
WorkManager JobScheduler/AlarmManager + executor n/a yes deferrable guaranteed work (A5)
Foreground service service in process n/a restartable user-visible long tasks (S1 chunk)

Pool facts: Dispatchers.Default size = max(2, CPU cores); Dispatchers.IO shares threads with Default, limit max(64, cores) (override with limitedParallelism). Choose IO for blocking calls, Default for CPU-bound, so CPU work does not starve on IO threads and vice versa.

Priority: threads default to the creator's priority; background pools should use Process.THREAD_PRIORITY_BACKGROUND so they do not steal CPU from the UI thread (Android also puts background cgroup threads on little cores).

Thread-confinement beats locks: confine state to one dispatcher (limitedParallelism(1), a Mutex, or an actor) rather than synchronizing everywhere.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
private val ioPool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4) { r ->
    Thread({ Process.setThreadPriority(Process.THREAD_PRIORITY_BACKGROUND); r.run() }, "io-worker")
}
val serialDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(1)   // ordered, off main

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Executors.newCachedThreadPool() for unbounded fan-out: hundreds of threads, memory and context-switch cost.
  • Blocking calls on Dispatchers.Default, starving CPU work.
  • Each library creating its own pool (OkHttp, Glide, Rx, custom) and the app having 100+ threads.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When HandlerThread over coroutines? → When an API demands a Handler/Looper (camera, sensors, MediaCodec callbacks) or strict message ordering with postDelayed.
  2. How do you cap total threads? → Share pools, set limitedParallelism, audit with adb shell ps -T <pid>.
  3. What does a thread cost? → About 1 MB virtual stack reservation by default for Java threads (plus kernel structures); on 32-bit processes thread count can hit limits (pthread_create failed).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: names coroutines and RxJava. Senior: gives a durability and lifecycle matrix, knows dispatcher sizing, priority and confinement, and watches thread counts.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A crash OutOfMemoryError: pthread_create failed on 32-bit devices came from three libraries each spawning unbounded cached pools.

questions.promptHtml: What is StrictMode, which policies does it have, and how do you use it responsibly in a team?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the cheapest tool for catching main-thread violations early; knowing its limits shows maturity.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: StrictMode is a developer tool that detects accidental disk, network and resource misuse on the main thread (ThreadPolicy) and leaks or insecure patterns process-wide (VmPolicy). I enable it in debug builds, with penaltyLog locally and penaltyDeath on CI/internal builds for new violations, and I never rely on it in production.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Two policies:

  • ThreadPolicy (per thread, usually main): detectDiskReads, detectDiskWrites, detectNetwork, detectCustomSlowCalls (+ StrictMode.noteSlowCall), detectResourceMismatches (API 23), detectUnbufferedIo (API 26), detectExplicitGc (API 28).
  • VmPolicy (process-wide): detectLeakedClosableObjects, detectLeakedSqlLiteObjects, detectActivityLeaks, detectLeakedRegistrationObjects, detectFileUriExposure, detectCleartextNetwork (API 23), detectContentUriWithoutPermission and detectUntaggedSockets (API 26), detectNonSdkApiUsage (API 28), detectImplicitDirectBoot (API 29), detectIncorrectContextUse (API 30), detectUnsafeIntentLaunch (API 31). Newer releases add more; check the class reference.

Penalties: penaltyLog, penaltyDeath, penaltyDeathOnNetwork, penaltyDialog, penaltyFlashScreen, penaltyDropBox, penaltyListener(executor, listener) (API 28, lets you forward violations to your logger).

How detection works: libcore/BlockGuard hooks (file and socket calls go through BlockGuard.getThreadPolicy()), which checks the calling thread's policy; so violations are caught only on the thread that has the policy set, and only for calls going through those hooks (not all native I/O, not memory-mapped reads, not Binder).

Limits: it detects the call, not the duration. A 1 ms read on a fast device is flagged and a 400 ms JNI call is not. Third-party SDK violations also trigger it; use permitDiskReads() scoped blocks with a comment, or a baseline allowlist.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) {
    StrictMode.setThreadPolicy(
        StrictMode.ThreadPolicy.Builder()
            .detectAll()
            .penaltyLog()
            .penaltyListener(Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor()) { v -> Log.e("Strict", "violation", v) }
            .build()
    )
    StrictMode.setVmPolicy(
        StrictMode.VmPolicy.Builder().detectLeakedClosableObjects().detectActivityLeaks()
            .detectLeakedRegistrationObjects().penaltyLog().build()
    )
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Enabling penaltyDeath globally with third-party SDKs and being unable to ship the debug build.
  • Setting the policy late (after content providers initialized) and missing startup violations; set it in Application.onCreate (or earlier via App Startup).
  • Treating a clean StrictMode run as proof of no jank.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does SharedPreferences show up? → Its first getX waits for the XML load (awaitLoadedLocked) and commit() writes synchronously; apply() is async but QueuedWork can still block onStop/onPause waits on ANR paths.
  2. Can you ship it in release? → Use penaltyListener only in internal/dogfood builds; overhead and noise are not acceptable for all users.
  3. How do you enforce in CI? → Instrumented tests with penaltyDeath for the main flows.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Enable detectAll in debug." Senior: knows the two policies, BlockGuard mechanism and its blind spots, uses listeners and CI death for ratcheting, and scopes exceptions deliberately.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Turning on detectDiskReads on a CI smoke test exposed 14 main-thread reads at startup; fixing them cut p90 cold start by about 180 ms on low-end phones.

questions.promptHtml: Where does the 5-second ANR limit come from, and what does the platform actually measure for input, broadcasts and services?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates say "main thread blocked 5 s". The real model is per-event timeouts with different triggers.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An ANR is not a general "main thread busy for 5 s" check. The platform tracks specific pending work with timeouts: for input, InputDispatcher waits for the app to acknowledge an event; 5 s without a response triggers an ANR. For broadcasts it is 10 s foreground and 60 s background, for services 20 s foreground and 200 s background, and about 10 s for ContentProvider publish. Then system_server collects stacks and shows the dialog.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Input ANR path:

  1. InputReader (native, system_server) reads events; InputDispatcher queues them per window/connection.
  2. Event is sent over an InputChannel socket to the app's InputEventReceiver, which the main Looper polls as an fd.
  3. App finishes the event and sends a "finished" signal back (finishInputEvent).
  4. If the oldest outstanding event for that connection is not finished within the timeout (default 5000 ms, DEFAULT_INPUT_DISPATCHING_TIMEOUT), InputDispatcher calls notifyAnr to ActivityManagerService.
  5. AMS dumps stacks (appears in /data/anr/ and logcat ANR in ...), kills the process or shows the dialog.

An input ANR can only occur when there is input to dispatch. A background-busy main thread with no touches produces no input ANR. Also "no focused window" can trigger an ANR if events wait 5 s with no focus target.

Timeouts (AMS constants, verify against current AOSP ActivityManagerService/ActiveServices/BroadcastConstants):

Trigger Timeout
Input event not acknowledged 5 s
Foreground broadcast onReceive 10 s
Background broadcast 60 s
Foreground service onCreate/onStartCommand 20 s
Background service 200 s
startForeground after startForegroundService short window (documented as ~5 s, AOSP constant differs by release; S1 chunk)
ContentProvider publish 10 s

Mechanism for broadcasts/services: AMS posts a delayed message (BROADCAST_TIMEOUT_MSG, SERVICE_TIMEOUT_MSG) when it hands off work and removes it when the app reports completion; if the message fires first, ANR. Measured end to end, including queueing in the app's main Looper, so a long earlier message counts against later work.

ANR rate is also a Play Console vitals metric (user-perceived ANR; bad behavior thresholds exist, verify current values on Play Console docs).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
adb logcat -b events | grep am_anr             # ANR events with process and reason
adb pull /data/anr/ .                          # needs root/debuggable on modern releases
adb bugreport                                  # includes ANR traces and main thread stack

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "5 s on main thread" for broadcast/service ANRs.
  • Assuming the culprit is the main-thread stack at ANR time; it might be a victim of a lock or Binder wait while the real cause was earlier.
  • Thinking goAsync() extends the limit indefinitely (S2 chunk covers it).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can an app be ANR'd while the stack at dump time is idle? → The blocking happened earlier; by the time stacks are dumped (later) the thread returned to Looper nativePollOnce. Look at CPU/lock info in the ANR header and earlier trace sections.
  2. Does a long frame cause an ANR? → Only if it delays an input ack past 5 s.
  3. Why do some ANRs mention "Waiting because the touched window has not finished processing certain input events"? → Input events queued behind an unacknowledged earlier event for the same connection.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "main thread blocked 5 s." Senior: lists per-component timeouts, explains the native InputDispatcher ack model, and explains why the dump may show an innocent stack.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 2% ANR rate was blamed on onTouch handlers; the actual cause was BroadcastReceivers queued behind a 30 s main-thread initializer, hitting the 10 s foreground broadcast limit.

questions.promptHtml: Describe the path of a touch event from the screen to your onTouchEvent, and what contributes to touch latency. What is MotionEvent batching?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Staff-level platform understanding: input is a pipeline across processes, not a callback.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The touch driver reports to the kernel, InputReader in system_server converts raw events, InputDispatcher picks the target window and sends it over an InputChannel socket to my app. My main Looper wakes on that fd, ViewRootImpl's input stages process it, and views see it. For MOVE events the app batches multiple samples per frame and delivers them aligned to Choreographer, so onTouchEvent receives one MotionEvent with historical samples per frame.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
touch panel (~120-240 Hz scan) -> kernel input driver -> /dev/input
 -> system_server: EventHub -> InputReader -> InputDispatcher
 -> (socketpair InputChannel) -> app: NativeInputEventReceiver (Looper fd)
 -> ViewRootImpl.WindowInputEventReceiver -> InputStages (early, view pre-IME, IME, native, view post-IME, synthetic)
 -> DecorView -> dispatchTouchEvent ...
 -> app calls finishInputEvent (ack back to InputDispatcher; ANR clock stops)

Batching: with ViewRootImpl input batching enabled (default), MOVE events that arrive between frames are buffered and delivered in CALLBACK_INPUT at the next vsync, not one at a time. The batched event carries getHistoricalX/Y/EventTime for the intermediate samples. Since Android 8-ish, resampling in the input consumer predicts position at frame time, reducing visible lag. DOWN/UP are delivered immediately.

Latency contributors: panel scan rate, kernel/driver, InputDispatcher, waiting for next vsync (avg half a frame: 8.3 ms at 60 Hz), main-thread busy time, draw pipeline (1-2 frames), SurfaceFlinger composition and panel scanout. Typical end-to-end is 50-100 ms on a 60 Hz phone, lower with high refresh.

Apps with ink/drawing needs use MotionEvent historical points, View.requestUnbufferedDispatch(event) (API 21) to bypass batching, or the Jetpack low-latency graphics libraries (androidx.graphics:graphics-core, front-buffered rendering). Stylus prediction uses androidx.input:input-motionprediction.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
override fun onTouchEvent(e: MotionEvent): Boolean {
    if (e.actionMasked == MotionEvent.ACTION_MOVE) {
        for (i in 0 until e.historySize) addPoint(e.getHistoricalX(i), e.getHistoricalY(i)) // missed samples
        addPoint(e.x, e.y)
    }
    return true
}
// Ask for events as they arrive (drawing apps):
// view.requestUnbufferedDispatch(motionEvent)  // on ACTION_DOWN

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Drawing only e.x/e.y in a drawing app and getting polygonal strokes at low frame rates.
  • Assuming one onTouchEvent call per hardware sample.
  • Doing heavy work in onTouchEvent; the ack waits for it, extending latency and risking input ANR.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why isn't the event delivered immediately for MOVE? → To align with vsync and avoid redundant redraws; delivering at 240 Hz would rerun the traversal needlessly.
  2. Where could the 5 s ANR clock be stuck? → Between dispatch and finishInputEvent, so slow handlers or main thread blocked.
  3. How do 120 Hz screens improve latency? → Half-period wait and shorter pipeline stages; touch sampling rate matters too (a 240 Hz touch panel improves it further).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Touch event goes to the Activity then views." Senior: describes cross-process InputChannel, ack protocol, batching with historical samples and the frame alignment, and knows the low-latency APIs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A signature capture screen had jagged curves on a 60 Hz tablet until the team consumed historical samples.

questions.promptHtml: Compare SurfaceView and TextureView from a threading and composition standpoint. When would you pick each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Video, camera and map/game views hit this choice; the answer reveals understanding of Surfaces, BufferQueues and SurfaceFlinger.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A SurfaceView owns a separate Surface that SurfaceFlinger composes as its own layer, so any thread can render into it without involving the View hierarchy; it is the most efficient and supports secure/DRM output. A TextureView renders into a SurfaceTexture and is drawn as part of the hardware-accelerated View tree, so it can be transformed, faded and scrolled like a normal view, at the cost of an extra GPU copy and more memory. I pick SurfaceView for video and games by default and TextureView only when I need view-level transforms or alpha in a scrolling or animated container.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
SurfaceView:  producer thread -> Surface (own BufferQueue) -> SurfaceFlinger layer
              (view hierarchy has a "hole" where the layer shows through)
TextureView:  producer thread -> SurfaceTexture -> RenderThread samples it as a GL texture
              inside the window's own surface (composited with the view tree)

Threading:

  • SurfaceView: you draw from any thread after surfaceCreated and must stop before surfaceDestroyed returns (the callbacks are on main; the Surface is invalid afterwards). Producer needs its own thread (game loop, MediaCodec/ExoPlayer renderer, camera).
  • TextureView: onSurfaceTextureAvailable/Destroyed/Updated callbacks run on the UI thread, but the producer still renders from its own thread. The consumer side (sampling the texture) happens on RenderThread during the window's draw, so the TextureView participates in the frame pipeline and requires hardware acceleration.

Trade-offs:

Aspect SurfaceView TextureView
Composition separate HWC layer, can use overlay, lower power GPU composited in view tree
Transform/alpha/animation supported on modern releases but with sync caveats; historically glitchy natural
Z-order punches a hole, behind/above window with setZOrderOnTop/MediaOverlay normal view order
Memory/latency lower extra buffer, ~1 frame more latency
DRM/secure content supported (setSecure) not for protected content on most devices
Lifecycle surface destroyed when invisible (on many releases) texture lives while attached

On Android 7.0 (API 24) SurfaceView position/size updates were synchronized with the View hierarchy, which removed most old "SurfaceView lags during scroll/animation" problems; older devices still show them.

In Compose, AndroidView can host either; newer Media3 has PlayerSurface composable that picks SurfaceView or TextureView.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class RenderView(ctx: Context) : SurfaceView(ctx), SurfaceHolder.Callback {
    @Volatile private var running = false
    private var thread: Thread? = null
    init { holder.addCallback(this) }
    override fun surfaceCreated(h: SurfaceHolder) {
        running = true
        thread = Thread {
            while (running) {
                val c = h.lockCanvas() ?: continue
                try { drawFrame(c) } finally { h.unlockCanvasAndPost(c) }
            }
        }.also { it.start() }
    }
    override fun surfaceChanged(h: SurfaceHolder, f: Int, w: Int, ht: Int) {}
    override fun surfaceDestroyed(h: SurfaceHolder) { running = false; thread?.join() } // must stop before returning
    private fun drawFrame(c: Canvas) { c.drawColor(Color.BLACK) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Touching the Surface after surfaceDestroyed (crash or IllegalArgumentException on post).
  • join()-ing a render thread that is blocked on main-thread work: deadlock.
  • Using TextureView for full-screen video and paying the extra GPU memory and battery for nothing.
  • Expecting SurfaceView to be captured by View.draw()/screenshots (it is a separate layer; use PixelCopy).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you screenshot a SurfaceView? → PixelCopy.request(surfaceView, bitmap, listener, handler) (API 24).
  2. Why is a TextureView blank when hardware acceleration is off? → It draws through the GL path; with software rendering it does not render.
  3. How does SurfaceFlinger decide overlay vs GPU composition? → HWC (Hardware Composer) assigns layers to display planes if constraints allow; a SurfaceView layer is more likely to qualify than a texture inside a window layer.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "TextureView is for animations, SurfaceView is faster." Senior: explains layer vs texture composition, which thread produces and which consumes, lifecycle contract, DRM/PixelCopy, and picks by requirements.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A camera preview inside a scrolling card used SurfaceView and tore during scroll on older devices; switching that one screen to TextureView fixed it with a measured +8% GPU use.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between invalidate(), postInvalidate() and requestLayout(), and how do they affect frame cost? What is layout thrashing?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Frame budget problems often come from unnecessary relayouts. This tests mechanism-level understanding of the View traversal.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: invalidate() marks a region dirty and causes a redraw (record display list) on the next frame; requestLayout() marks the view and its ancestors for remeasure and relayout and then redraw, which is far more expensive. postInvalidate() is the thread-safe version of invalidate() for non-UI threads. Layout thrashing is changing layout-affecting properties repeatedly, or reading and writing in a loop, so layouts run multiple times or every frame.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• invalidate(): sets dirty flags up the parent chain, calls ViewRootImpl.scheduleTraversals(). Only draw re-runs for dirty views; with hardware acceleration only affected RenderNodes re-record. Must be called on the UI thread.
  • postInvalidate(): posts to the UI thread via the ViewRootImpl handler (ViewRootImpl.dispatchInvalidateDelayed). Safe from other threads.
  • requestLayout(): sets PFLAG_FORCE_LAYOUT on the view and all parents up to the root, so the next traversal runs measure and layout for that subtree path, then draw. Cost scales with hierarchy depth and with double-measure layouts (nested weighted LinearLayout, RelativeLayout, ConstraintLayout with chains and barriers).
  • Property changes that call requestLayout: setText on a wrap_content TextView, setLayoutParams, setVisibility(GONE/VISIBLE) changes, image size changes.
  • Property changes that only invalidate: color, setAlpha, translation/scale/rotation (RenderNode properties, no re-record at all in many cases).

Layout thrash patterns:

  1. Setting text in onBindViewHolder for 20 visible rows while each triggers parent relayout.
  2. Calling requestLayout() inside onLayout/onMeasure, re-triggering a second traversal; Android logs requestLayout() improperly called during layout.
  3. Animating layoutParams.width per frame.
  4. Reading view.measuredHeight after write inside a loop forcing synchronous layout (measure() manual calls).

Mitigations: fixed-size or layout_height constants when possible; RecyclerView.setHasFixedSize(true) when adapter changes don't alter size; animate transforms not layout; TextView with precomputed text (PrecomputedTextCompat) off main; flatten hierarchies; use ViewStub.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Costly: one layout per frame for 300 ms
ValueAnimator.ofInt(startH, endH).apply {
    addUpdateListener { v -> view.updateLayoutParams { height = v.animatedValue as Int } }
    start()
}
// Cheaper: animate a transform, resolve layout once at the end
view.animate().scaleY(0.5f).withEndAction { view.updateLayoutParams { height = endH }; view.scaleY = 1f }.start()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling invalidate() from a background thread (CalledFromWrongThreadException).
  • Calling requestLayout() when only invalidate() is needed, e.g. after changing a paint color.
  • Assuming GONE is free; it removes the view from layout and requires parent relayout (INVISIBLE keeps layout, View.setAlpha(0) too).
  • Many invalidate() calls per frame are cheap because they coalesce; many requestLayout() calls also coalesce, but each traversal still pays for the whole dirty subtree.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is invalidate(Rect) vs full? → Dirty rect limits redraw region for software rendering; with hardware acceleration the whole RenderNode re-records but GPU clip still applies.
  2. How do you diagnose layout cost? → Perfetto/System trace slices measure/layout, Layout Inspector, Android Studio profiler; playbook in A6.
  3. How does RecyclerView avoid relayout on scroll? → It recycles and binds without full-parent relayout; scrolling uses offsetChildren; requestLayout only on adapter dataset changes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "invalidate redraws, requestLayout remeasures." Senior: relates each to the traversal stages, knows which properties trigger which, identifies thrash patterns, and picks transforms over layout animation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A collapsible header animated height every frame in a heavy ConstraintLayout and cost about 9 ms per frame on mid-tier devices; switching to translation plus a final layout pass brought it under 3 ms.

questions.promptHtml: How can you measure frame performance from inside the app in production, and what do "slow" and "frozen" frames mean?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows you treat jank as telemetry, not a feeling. (Deep trace analysis belongs to A6.)

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I use the platform's FrameMetrics API (API 24) or the Jetpack JankStats library, which hook per-frame timing and report janky frames with the UI state at the time. Play Console classifies frames over 16 ms as slow and over 700 ms as frozen. I sample in production, attach the screen name and scroll state, and track the janky-frame percentage per screen.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Window.addOnFrameMetricsAvailableListener(listener, handler) (API 24) delivers a FrameMetrics per frame with durations: input handling, animation, layout/measure, draw, sync, command issue, swap buffers, TOTAL_DURATION, and intended vs actual vsync (INTENDED_VSYNC_TIMESTAMP, VSYNC_TIMESTAMP; deadline-related fields from API 31). Callbacks come on the handler you provide, so use a background HandlerThread.

FrameMetrics.TOTAL_DURATION =
  input + animation + layout_measure + draw + sync_queue + sync + command_issue + swap_buffers + gpu(API 31)
jank if TOTAL_DURATION > frame budget (or deadline missed)

Jetpack JankStats (androidx.metrics:metrics-performance) wraps FrameMetrics on API 16+ with different internal sources, supports PerformanceMetricsState so you attach key/value state like "screen" -> "Feed", and gives FrameData(frameStartNanos, frameDurationUiNanos, isJank, states).

Definitions (Play vitals / Android vitals): slow frame renders > 16 ms (at 60 Hz reference), frozen frame > 700 ms. Percent of "slow" or "frozen" sessions are tracked; keep numbers as relative signals. Use dumpsys gfxinfo <pkg> for quick lab histograms (Janky frames, percentiles) and Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric in CI.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class FrameReporter(private val window: Window) {
    private val thread = HandlerThread("frames").apply { start() }
    private val listener = Window.OnFrameMetricsAvailableListener { _, fm, _ ->
        val totalMs = fm.getMetric(FrameMetrics.TOTAL_DURATION) / 1_000_000.0
        if (totalMs > 16.7) Log.w("Frame", "slow %.1f ms, layout=%d us".format(totalMs,
            fm.getMetric(FrameMetrics.LAYOUT_MEASURE_DURATION) / 1000))
    }
    fun start() = window.addOnFrameMetricsAvailableListener(listener, Handler(thread.looper))
    fun stop() = window.removeOnFrameMetricsAvailableListener(listener)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Receiving the listener on the main handler (adds overhead and skews results).
  • Judging with a 16.7 ms threshold on 90/120 Hz.
  • Forgetting to remove the listener (leaks the Window/Activity).
  • Reporting every frame to analytics; aggregate on device first.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. FrameMetrics vs Choreographer.FrameCallback? → FrameMetrics gives per-stage durations including RenderThread; Choreographer only vsync timestamps.
  2. Why might lab and field janky percentages differ? → Device mix, thermals, background load, data volume; so segment by device tier and OS.
  3. What frozen frames usually mean? → Blocking I/O, locks, big synchronous inflation or GC; not GPU.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: uses the profiler once. Senior: builds production telemetry with JankStats, attaches state, thresholds by refresh rate, and gates releases with Macrobenchmark.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Per-screen janky-frame telemetry flagged a settings screen at 31% jank on low-tier devices, caused by a synchronous SharedPreferences migration, invisible in manual testing.

questions.contextHtml:
A junior's PR for a "recent searches" feature passes review and QA on a Pixel 8. After release, vitals show cold-start p90 up from 1.9 s to 2.7 s on devices with 2-3 GB RAM and slow eMMC storage; ANR rate rises from 0.2% to 0.5%. The code:

class SearchActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private val prefs by lazy { getSharedPreferences("search", MODE_PRIVATE) }

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContentView(R.layout.activity_search)
        val saved = prefs.getString("recent", "[]")!!          // 1
        recent.addAll(Json.decodeFromString<List<String>>(saved))
        File(cacheDir, "suggest.db").copyTo(File(filesDir, "suggest.db"), overwrite = true) // 2
    }

    fun addRecent(q: String) {
        recent.add(0, q)
        prefs.edit().putString("recent", Json.encodeToString(recent)).commit()   // 3
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find what is wrong, explain the impact and how you would prevent a recurrence.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use apply() instead of commit()." That fixes one line, misses that the first read and the file copy are on main and that the problem generalizes; no prevention plan.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What size is suggest.db (2 MB or 80 MB)? How big can recent grow? Is the ANR from input, broadcast or startup? Are slow-storage devices overrepresented? These tell me whether the cost is I/O bound or CPU.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix by moving (2) off main and making (3) apply(); staged rollout to 10% first. Roll back if the feature is flagged.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) File copy on main: big sequential read+write, hundreds of ms on slow flash. (b) First SharedPreferences access loads and parses the whole XML file synchronously (awaitLoadedLocked). (c) commit() blocks for fsync on every add. (d) JSON decode of a large list. Red herring: the layout inflate, which was unchanged.
  4. How I'd verify each: Enable StrictMode with detectDiskReads/Writes and penaltyLog in a debug build on a low-end device; it flags all three lines. Capture a Perfetto trace of cold start and look for fsync/read on the main thread and Contending for or Lock contention slices. Measure startup with adb shell am start -W.
  5. Root cause: Three kinds of disk I/O on the main thread in onCreate, each blocking with unbounded latency on slow flash; commit() also does a synchronous write, and the shared QueuedWork can delay the next lifecycle step.
  6. Fix: Short term: wrap in a coroutine.
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    setContentView(R.layout.activity_search)
    lifecycleScope.launch {
        val list = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
            File(cacheDir, "suggest.db").copyTo(File(filesDir, "suggest.db"), overwrite = true)
            Json.decodeFromString<List<String>>(prefs.getString("recent", "[]")!!)
        }
        recent.addAll(list); adapter.notifyDataSetChanged()
    }
}

Long term: migrate to Jetpack DataStore (async by design) or Room; do not copy databases at startup, ship or download once. 7. Prevention: StrictMode penaltyDeath in debug and in instrumented CI tests; a lint/Detekt rule flagging commit() and file APIs outside IO; performance budget check with Macrobenchmark startup; code review checklist "any I/O on main?". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just wrap everything in Thread {}, since this gives races with UI state. I would not remove StrictMode violations by permitAll(). I would not use apply() and assume it is free: pending apply() writes are awaited in onStop via QueuedWork, which can still ANR if backlogged.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if StrictMode is clean but startup is still slow? → Violations only flag calls through BlockGuard; native I/O, mmap and Binder are not flagged. Use a trace.
  • Why is apply() safer but not safe? → It writes asynchronously but QueuedWork.waitToFinish() blocks on lifecycle transitions.
  • Is DataStore safe for "read before first frame"? → Not synchronous; show a placeholder and update, or preload in Application on a background thread.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A search-history feature copied a 40 MB seed database in onCreate. It looked fine in QA on flagship hardware; on 32 GB eMMC phones it took 1.5 s, and 3% of sessions ANR'd. A one-line StrictMode config in CI would have caught it on day one.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only changes commit() to apply(), or says "it is fine, I/O is small".
  • Hire: finds all three main-thread I/O sites, moves them to IO, mentions StrictMode.
  • Strong hire: also explains first-load SharedPreferences, QueuedWork behavior, DataStore migration, CI enforcement and rollout plan.

questions.contextHtml:
An app shows a vertical NestedScrollView feed that contains a horizontal "stories" RecyclerView. QA reports that on some devices horizontal swipes feel "sticky": 1 in 3 swipes scroll the page vertically instead of the carousel, especially when the swipe is slightly diagonal. Analytics: carousel engagement dropped 18% since the redesign that moved the carousel inside the page. The developer's fix:

class StoriesRecyclerView(ctx: Context, attrs: AttributeSet) : RecyclerView(ctx, attrs) {
    override fun onTouchEvent(e: MotionEvent): Boolean {
        parent.requestDisallowInterceptTouchEvent(true)   // always
        return super.onTouchEvent(e)
    }
}

After that fix, vertical scroll starting on the carousel is dead, and users complain they cannot scroll the feed when their finger starts on stories. Another dev proposes overriding onInterceptTouchEvent in the NestedScrollView to return true when |dx| > |dy|.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong with both attempts and how should it be solved?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Set requestDisallowInterceptTouchEvent(true) on the parent" or "use onInterceptTouchEvent". Doesn't distinguish direction, DOWN vs MOVE, or realize that nested scrolling already handles the case.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which versions of RecyclerView/NestedScrollView/AndroidX? Is the carousel a ViewPager2 (it has its own nested-scroll workaround) or a RecyclerView? Is any parent custom? Does it only occur on certain devices (touch slop varies with density)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert the always-disallow fix, since it disables vertical scrolling over a large part of the feed; ship the previous behavior while fixing.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Angle test: vertical slop is reached before the horizontal one with diagonal finger paths. (b) Parent steals the gesture because the child hasn't claimed it yet. (c) The parent's onInterceptTouchEvent intercepts once vertical movement passes slop. Red herring: device-specific frame drops.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log actionMasked, dx, dy and which view's onInterceptTouchEvent returns true; use adb shell getevent/Show touches; test with a 10-20 degree diagonal swipe on a physical device; check ViewConfiguration.scaledTouchSlop per device.
  5. Root cause: The fix calls disallow on every event including the first DOWN and all vertical drags, so the parent never gets the gesture. The parent-side interception alternative returns true early and then the carousel gets ACTION_CANCEL (no more horizontal scrolling for that gesture), and also fights the nested-scroll connection.
  6. Fix: Decide by direction after touch slop, only then disallow, and let the gesture reset naturally (the flag is cleared on next DOWN).
override fun onInterceptTouchEvent(e: MotionEvent): Boolean {
    when (e.actionMasked) {
        MotionEvent.ACTION_DOWN -> { startX = e.x; startY = e.y }
        MotionEvent.ACTION_MOVE -> {
            val dx = abs(e.x - startX); val dy = abs(e.y - startY)
            if (dx > touchSlop && dx > dy * 1.2f) parent.requestDisallowInterceptTouchEvent(true)
            else if (dy > touchSlop && dy > dx) parent.requestDisallowInterceptTouchEvent(false)
        }
    }
    return super.onInterceptTouchEvent(e)
}

Long term: rely on nested scrolling; the carousel is horizontal-only so canScrollHorizontally plus direction check is enough. If it is a ViewPager2, use the documented NestedScrollableHost pattern. 7. Prevention: Gesture test on instrumented UI (GeneralSwipeAction with diagonal vectors); manual gesture matrix in QA across densities; do not nest same-direction scrollers. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not intercept at the NestedScrollView level (it must understand every child). I would not add per-device slop hacks. The 1.2 ratio is a heuristic, tune with telemetry.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not disallow only on ACTION_DOWN? → Direction is unknown at DOWN, and the flag then blocks vertical drags.
  • Compose carousel inside a vertical scroll? → Compose uses nested scroll with consumption; conflict is rare, see A3.
  • Accessibility (TalkBack) swipe? → Scroll actions come via accessibility actions, not touch dispatch; implement AccessibilityActions.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "just always disallow" fix for a map embedded in a scroll page worked in the demo and killed page scrolling for 40% of the screen; the right behavior was direction-aware and only for two-finger map gestures.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: toggles the flag blindly or returns true everywhere.
  • Hire: direction check after slop, explains CANCEL and flag reset.
  • Strong hire: prefers nested scrolling, tests diagonals, explains why parent interception is wrong, and has a rollout/revert plan.

questions.contextHtml:
A ride-hailing app (4M DAU, 60% on Android 11-14, 35% on 3 GB RAM devices) sees ANR rate jump from 0.25% to 1.1% overnight after release 8.41. Play Console clusters: Input dispatching timed out (… Waiting because the focused window has not finished processing the input event). The main-thread stack in the traces:

"main" prio=5 tid=1 Waiting
  at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(Native Method)
  at java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport.park
  at com.app.location.LocationCache.get(LocationCache.kt:44)   // synchronized(lock)
  at com.app.map.MapPresenter.onCameraIdle(MapPresenter.kt:112)
"DefaultDispatcher-worker-3" Blocked
  at com.app.location.LocationCache.refresh(LocationCache.kt:88)  // holding lock
  at android.os.BinderProxy.transactNative
  at android.location.ILocationManager$Stub$Proxy.getLastLocation

Release 8.41 added a periodic location refresh every 5 s on a worker. Crash-free is unaffected. The release also upgraded OkHttp and moved image loading to a new library.
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through diagnosis, mitigation and the permanent fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Move the map code to a background thread" or "blame the OkHttp upgrade". Ignores that main waits on a lock held across a Binder call, and does not use data to rank hypotheses.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the ANR concentrated on specific OEMs/OS (system_server location HAL slowness)? Time from lock acquisition to release in the field? Does it correlate with users in poor GPS/tunnel conditions? Did refresh frequency change per device or by remote config? Which stacks hold the lock when ANR hits?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Kill-switch the 5 s periodic refresh via remote config (or lengthen to 60 s); if no flag, hotfix to non-blocking read. Staged rollout halt on 8.41.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Lock held across a blocking Binder call (getLastLocation) on the worker; main contends for the same monitor. (b) Binder thread pool exhaustion in system_server on weak devices making the call slow. (c) OkHttp/image library spikes (red herring: no main-thread frames in them). (d) GC pauses (concurrent copying means short pauses; unlikely to hold 5 s).
  4. How I'd verify each: From traces, check which thread owns the monitor (- waiting to lock <0x...> held by thread 41) and what that thread is doing (Binder transact). Segment ANR by OEM/OS in Play Console and Firebase Crashlytics ANR reports; reproduce by adding artificial Thread.sleep(6000) to the fake getLastLocation with the lock held; add StrictMode custom slow calls; Perfetto on a repro showing monitor contention with owner slices and binder transaction duration.
  5. Root cause: The cache serialized readers and the writer on one synchronized lock and the writer held it while making a synchronous Binder call that can take seconds. Main thread's get() needed the same lock, so a slow system service call turned into a 5 s unacknowledged input event.
  6. Fix: Never hold a lock across I/O or IPC; keep only a volatile snapshot readable without waiting.
class LocationCache(private val lm: LocationProvider) {
    @Volatile private var snapshot: Location? = null
    fun get(): Location? = snapshot                         // lock-free read on main
    suspend fun refresh() {                                  // runs on IO
        val fresh = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { lm.lastLocationBlocking() }
        snapshot = fresh
    }
}

Also use FusedLocationProviderClient callbacks instead of polling, and add a timeout (withTimeout) to refresh. 7. Prevention: Static rule: no synchronized blocks around IPC/I/O; lock-contention alerting through ANR clustering by top frames; Macrobenchmark with injected slow dependencies; ANR rate as a release gate in staged rollout (halt at 2x baseline). 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not raise timeouts (they are platform constants). I would not simply move onCameraIdle off main: it updates UI state. A volatile snapshot can be slightly stale; acceptable for this map.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the trace shows main in BinderProxy.transactNative instead? → The main thread made the IPC itself; move the call off main or use async APIs; check system_server load.
  • What if the worker holds a ReentrantLock instead? → Same contention; the trace names the owner via held by. Prefer immutable snapshots.
  • How do you separate your fault from the OS's? → If many apps' ANRs line up in the same device/OS version windows, system_server pressure is involved; still design not to block.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "tiny" cache with a coarse lock produced a 1% ANR regression only on low-RAM devices where the system service was slow; reads were lock-free after the fix and the rate returned to baseline within a day of staged rollout.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: random moves to background threads or blames libraries without evidence.
  • Hire: reads the trace, identifies lock-over-Binder, fixes with non-blocking read.
  • Strong hire: ranks hypotheses with data, explains the input ack model, adds release gating and static prevention, and discusses staleness trade-offs.

questions.contextHtml:
A fintech app animates a "balance count-up" and a custom pull-to-refresh with this logic, tuned in 2020 on 60 Hz devices:

private val handler = Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())
private var step = 0
private val tick = object : Runnable {
    override fun run() {
        step++
        progress = (step / 18f).coerceAtMost(1f)       // 18 steps * 16 ms ~ 300 ms
        invalidate()
        if (progress < 1f) handler.postDelayed(this, 16)
    }
}

After the new flagship phones (120 Hz, 18% of DAU) arrived, support tickets say the animation "judders and runs slow". Perfetto shows the animation taking ~510 ms on those devices and visibly uneven frames; on 60 Hz devices it takes ~300-320 ms. Another report: on battery-saver (reduced refresh 60 Hz) it's fine. Product wants animations to be exactly 300 ms everywhere.
questions.promptHtml: Explain what is happening and how you would re-implement it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use postDelayed(8) for 120 Hz." Hardcodes another rate; ignores that the delay is not aligned to vsync and that rates vary dynamically.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the panel use adaptive refresh (LTPO 1-120 Hz) so the rate changes during the animation? Is the 510 ms measured from first to last frame or including a delay at start? Are other animations using ValueAnimator also off? Are the failing devices throttling thermally?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Switch the two animations to ValueAnimator/ObjectAnimator with a 300 ms duration (a one-line-class change), which is time-based and vsync-aligned; ship as a hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) postDelayed(16) isn't frame-aligned: with an 8.3 ms vsync period each tick lands on every second or third frame, so step timing drifts (16 ms delay plus scheduling delay > 16.6 ms, up to ~25 ms), which stretches 18 steps to ~450-510 ms. (b) Steps are frame-count based, not time based. (c) invalidate() per tick with other main-thread work pushes ticks later. Red herring: GC, which is not visible in the trace.
  4. How I'd verify each: Perfetto frame timeline on a 120 Hz device shows irregular frame intervals aligned to ticks, 8.3 ms vsyncs with the animation updating only on some; log SystemClock.uptimeMillis() per tick; compare with a ValueAnimator run; adb shell settings put system peak_refresh_rate 120/min_refresh_rate to force rates on a test device; dumpsys display for active mode.
  5. Root cause: The animation is driven by a timer that assumes a 16 ms frame and by a step counter, not by elapsed time or by Choreographer. At 120 Hz a 16 ms delay does not align with vsync (8.3 ms), so updates land unevenly (judder); with handler scheduling slop the total time inflates. It looked "right" at 60 Hz only because 16 ms ~ one frame.
  6. Fix: Drive progress from the frame clock and elapsed time.
private var startNanos = 0L
private val frame = object : Choreographer.FrameCallback {
    override fun doFrame(frameTimeNanos: Long) {
        if (startNanos == 0L) startNanos = frameTimeNanos
        progress = ((frameTimeNanos - startNanos) / 300_000_000f).coerceIn(0f, 1f)
        invalidate()
        if (progress < 1f) Choreographer.getInstance().postFrameCallback(this) else startNanos = 0L
    }
}
// Simpler: ValueAnimator.ofFloat(0f, 1f).setDuration(300).apply { addUpdateListener { progress = it.animatedFraction; invalidate() } }.start()
  1. Prevention: Lint/review rule: no postDelayed loops for animation; add 120 Hz device in test lab; Macrobenchmark with FrameTimingMetric on 60 and 120 Hz; check "animator duration scale" in developer options during QA (system ANIMATOR_DURATION_SCALE of 0 should still work).
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not set Surface.setFrameRate as a workaround, since the problem is timing source. I would not special-case rates. Time-based animation may skip frames when busy (acceptable, the end state is right). Respect reduced-motion preferences (animator scale 0 gives instant completion for ValueAnimator).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why use frameTimeNanos and not System.nanoTime()? → It is the vsync time, identical for all callbacks in the frame, giving consistent steps and avoiding jitter.
  • What if the main thread stalls 200 ms mid-animation? → Time-based progress jumps ahead, completing on schedule rather than slowly replaying frames.
  • Compose equivalent? → animateFloatAsState/Animatable use the monotonic frame clock; no manual timers (A3).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A hand-rolled spinner using postDelayed(16) ran at three different speeds across a fleet (60, 90, 120 Hz) and slower under battery saver; replacing it with an Animator removed the discrepancy and 14 lines of code.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: changes the delay constant per refresh rate.
  • Hire: moves to time-based animation using ValueAnimator or Choreographer.
  • Strong hire: explains vsync alignment math, adaptive refresh, frameTimeNanos, verifies with Perfetto, adds 120 Hz to the test matrix and reduced-motion handling.

questions.contextHtml: A 9-year-old Java/Kotlin app (6M MAU, 70 screens) still has 214 AsyncTask subclasses, many as non-static inner classes of Activities. Crashlytics: 0.4% of sessions crash with IllegalStateException / NullPointerException in onPostExecute after rotation or back press, and RejectedExecutionException: Task rejected from ThreadPoolExecutor ... queued tasks = 128 (about 600/day) in the image-grid screen. The team wants to target a newer SDK, drop AsyncTask, and has one quarter with 3 engineers; feature delivery must continue; there is no good test coverage. Leadership asks for a plan and a definition of "done".
questions.promptHtml: How do you migrate without a big-bang rewrite and without regressions?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Replace them all with coroutines this sprint." Ignores risk, ordering semantics (serial executor), cancellation behavior, and the absence of tests.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do any tasks depend on serial ordering (default executor was serial)? Which tasks outlive the screen on purpose? Is there Java-only code (no coroutines)? Which screens are highest traffic and crash? Is Kotlin/coroutines/ViewModel already on the classpath?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the top two crashers first: the 128-queue rejection (image grid: add a bounded, dedicated loader or the existing image library with a proper pool) and the post-destroy callbacks (null/isDestroyed guards, as a stopgap on the five worst screens). This reduces crash noise before refactoring.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: For the crashes: (a) onPostExecute runs after Activity destroyed or view nulled; (b) fire-and-forget tasks enqueued per row; (c) tasks relying on shared state with implicit serial ordering; (d) tasks that must finish (writes) being killed on rotation. Red herring: "AsyncTask is slow", since the problem is lifecycle, not speed.
  4. How I'd verify each: Group Crashlytics by class and callback; grep call sites execute(/executeOnExecutor(; categorize tasks into three buckets (UI-bound load, fire-and-forget write, long-running/must-finish); add temporary logging for ordering; reproduce with "Don't keep activities" and rotation; run Android lint and StrictMode on top screens.
  5. Root cause: Pre-lifecycle-era concurrency primitive tied to Activity references, with unstructured completion callbacks and an implicit serial/bounded executor, so destruction races and queue saturation are inevitable.
  6. Fix: Strangler approach.
    • Phase 0: ban new AsyncTask (lint rule); add a thin BackgroundRunner wrapper with Executor + main-thread callback for Java call sites, so each migration is mechanical.
    • Phase 1: UI-bound loads move to ViewModel + viewModelScope.launch { withContext(IO) } with state exposed as StateFlow; tackle highest-crash screens first.
    • Phase 2: fire-and-forget/must-finish work moves to WorkManager (A5) or an application-scoped scope with explicit supervisor, not a screen scope.
    • Phase 3: delete remaining tasks; remove the wrapper.
class SearchViewModel(private val repo: Repo) : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow<UiState>(UiState.Loading)
    val state: StateFlow<UiState> = _state
    fun load(q: String) = viewModelScope.launch {
        _state.value = runCatching { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { repo.search(q) } }
            .fold({ UiState.Data(it) }, { UiState.Error(it) })
    }
}

Where serial ordering mattered, use Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(1) or a Mutex. 7. Prevention: Custom lint/Detekt rule failing on android.os.AsyncTask imports; burn-down dashboard (214 to 0) with weekly reporting; characterization tests (Robolectric/instrumented) around each migrated screen using the same inputs; feature-flag/stage rollouts of migrated screens to 5% then 50%. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not auto-convert with a script and merge in one PR. I would not wrap AsyncTask semantic copies in coroutines using GlobalScope. I would accept that screens with state restoration tests take longer; the order is crash-rate first, not alphabetical.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A task writes to disk and must finish when the user leaves. → That is not screen work; use WorkManager or an app-scope job with a durable queue.
  • Java-only module? → Executors + Handler/ListenableFuture or a Kotlin-coroutines bridge; do not block migration on language adoption.
  • How do you prove no behavior regressions? → Characterization tests, side-by-side counters (old vs new path outputs) in a flagged shadow run, plus crash and ANR deltas per cohort.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A migration plan sorted by crash count rather than by code area retired 60% of the AsyncTask-related crashes after only 20% of the call sites had been converted, which kept leadership's support for the long tail.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: big-bang rewrite, no risk plan.
  • Hire: buckets tasks, uses ViewModel + coroutines, ranks by crash impact.
  • Strong hire: preserves ordering semantics, separates must-finish work to WorkManager, adds lint ban, shadow/flagged rollout and burn-down metrics.

questions.contextHtml: You are building a short-video feed (like a vertical pager, 8M DAU, 55% devices with 3-4 GB RAM, p95 swipe-to-first-frame target 250 ms). A prototype uses TextureView per page inside ViewPager2, with a single ExoPlayer instance per visible page.
