Complaints: heat and battery drain (+11% battery per hour of use vs competitor), memory of ~45 MB extra, and sometimes a black frame flash when swiping. A staff engineer proposes switching to SurfaceView everywhere; the designer wants a crossfade and rounded corners with a scale-down "peek" animation when opening comments.
questions.promptHtml: Which view type and structure do you choose, and what do you do about the animations and the black flashes?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "SurfaceView is faster, use it everywhere" or "TextureView because it animates." No awareness of composition cost, lifecycle, black flash causes, or per-page instance counts.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is content DRM-protected? Do we need the preview of the next page while swiping (two surfaces live)? Minimum API level? Do rounded corners need to be on video itself? How often is the "peek" used (hot path or rare)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Keep the current build but release players and surfaces for pages beyond the +/-1 window and set setKeepContentOnPlayerReset-like shutter behavior (Media3 PlayerView shutter / keep last frame) to cover the black flash while a decision is made.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) TextureView adds GPU copy and extra buffering (power + memory) for every page; (b) black flash from the Surface being destroyed/recreated on page transitions or a missing shutter; (c) too many live decoders/surfaces; (d) GC or main-thread layout jitter (red herring unless traces show it).
  4. How I'd verify each: Perfetto (SurfaceFlinger layers, GPU frame time), dumpsys SurfaceFlinger to see layers and composition type (HWC vs GPU), dumpsys meminfo for graphics memory, battery historian or measured power with a controlled 30 minute run; log surfaceCreated/Destroyed timing against the flash.
  5. Root cause: Choosing the surface type by convenience: TextureView forces the video through the GPU composition path with an extra copy, while SurfaceView can use a hardware overlay layer. The black flashes come from surface lifecycle mismatch rather than the type itself.
  6. Fix: Default to SurfaceView for the playing page (best power, supports secure content); keep the pager but attach the player's surface only to the settled page, with a thumbnail/frame placeholder (ImageView) overlaid until onRenderedFirstFrame. For the crossfade and the peek scale: do them on the placeholder/thumbnail snapshot, or temporarily swap to TextureView only during the rare peek animation (or use a freeze frame via PixelCopy from the SurfaceView, API 24). Rounded corners: clip via an overlay mask, since clipToOutline on SurfaceView has limits on older releases; verify on target devices.
playerView.setShutterBackgroundColor(Color.TRANSPARENT)
player.addListener(object : Player.Listener {
    override fun onRenderedFirstFrame() { thumbnail.visibility = View.GONE }
})
// when surface will be detached for the next page:
thumbnail.setImageBitmap(captureWithPixelCopy(surfaceView)) // keep last frame
  1. Prevention: Perf benchmark job: 30 minute scroll session on a 3 GB device recording battery, GPU memory and first-frame latency; metrics gate for first-frame p95; a lifecycle test for surface destroyed/recreated.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use TextureView for all pages "for the animations". I would not keep more than two decoders/surfaces alive on low-RAM devices. The SurfaceView plan costs complexity (placeholder choreography); I accept it for the battery win.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the product requires picture-in-picture-like draggable video? → Draggable overlays work with SurfaceView on modern releases (position-synced since API 24), but verify on target devices; fall back to TextureView for that mode only.
  • Why does SurfaceView sometimes show a black frame on resume? → The Surface is recreated when the window is shown again; keep a placeholder until the first rendered frame.
  • Does Compose change it? → Use Media3's Compose PlayerSurface with SURFACE_TYPE_SURFACE_VIEW unless you need transforms, see A3.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Swapping the playing page from TextureView to SurfaceView cut GPU memory by about 40 MB and 6-8% hourly battery on mid-tier devices, while a snapshot trick kept the crossfade the designer wanted.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks one view type without trade-offs.
  • Hire: SurfaceView for efficiency, TextureView for transforms, and mentions placeholder for flash.
  • Strong hire: explains composition paths, measures with SurfaceFlinger/Perfetto, limits live surfaces, handles DRM, and designs animation with snapshots or targeted fallback.

questions.contextHtml: Post-incident review for last week's incident: release 5.12 of a retail app (1.8M DAU) saw ANR rate rise from 0.3% to 0.9% for 36 hours. The on-call engineer saw in logcat on their own device Choreographer: Skipped 47 frames! The application may be doing too much work on its main thread at startup, spent two days optimizing Application.onCreate (saved 120 ms), but the ANR rate did not change. Play Console clusters showed Broadcast of Intent { act=android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED } and executing service com.app/.SyncService ANRs, mostly background, mostly on Android 13 devices from two OEMs. The real fix, found by someone else on day three, was a receiver doing a 14 s synchronous database migration inside onReceive. Management asks: why did it take three days, and how do we avoid it?
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: what went wrong in the investigation, and what is the technical and process fix?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "We should optimize startup more" or "blame the on-call". Doesn't recognize the log line is a red herring unrelated to broadcast ANR timeouts, nor the lack of triage by ANR type.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What exactly was the ANR type breakdown (input / broadcast / service) and what fraction was foreground? Which timeline did the ANR spike start vs release start? Did the engineer check the Play Console ANR clusters before profiling? What did the DB migration run on, and why was it in a receiver?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt rollout at 5.12; move migration out of onReceive (hotfix: start a worker/ foreground-appropriate path); if the receiver is not essential, disable it via component state toggle in a quick patch.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) A receiver blocking main past the broadcast timeout (10 s foreground / 60 s background): matches Broadcast of Intent text. (b) The service ANR is a second symptom of the same main-thread being busy (service callbacks queued behind the migration). (c) Startup cost (red herring: "Skipped 47 frames" is a Choreographer warning about a late frame, it does not cause an ANR by itself and was measured on a dev device). (d) OEM-specific boot behavior.
  4. How I'd verify each: Read the ANR reason string and top frames; correlate with BOOT_COMPLETED at device boot (many apps start at once, system is slow); reproduce via adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED -p com.app (and adb reboot on an Android 13 device); add StrictMode and a timer around onReceive; Perfetto trace of boot period.
  5. Root cause: onReceive runs on the main thread and the platform measures broadcast completion with a timeout, so a 14 s synchronous operation exceeded 10 s (foreground) or queued other broadcasts and service starts behind it. Investigation root cause: they treated a generic jank log line as the incident instead of classifying the ANR type first.
  6. Fix: Technical: receiver does only a cheap enqueue.
class BootReceiver : BroadcastReceiver() {
    override fun onReceive(ctx: Context, intent: Intent) {
        val pending = goAsync()                    // still has to finish within the limit
        CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.Default).launch {
            try { WorkManager.getInstance(ctx).enqueueUniqueWork("migrate",
                    ExistingWorkPolicy.KEEP, OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<MigrateWorker>().build()) }
            finally { pending.finish() }
        }
    }
}

The migration itself moves to a Worker (A5) with progress and retry. 7. Prevention: Runbook step 1 is "classify by ANR type and trigger in Play Console before profiling"; dashboards by type; release gates on ANR deltas; lint rule against file/DB APIs in onReceive; instrumented test that times receivers with a 1 s budget; blameless review wording focusing on process (missing triage step), not the engineer. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not extend startup optimization as the response. I would not use goAsync() to just stretch to the limit with 14 s work. I would not remove the migration without a plan for users who haven't migrated.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why were the ANRs mostly background? → Background broadcasts have the longer 60 s limit but still ANR; on boot the receiver ran while the process was cold-starting under load.
  • Is Skipped N frames ever actionable? → Yes for jank signal and startup frames, but never as ANR evidence on its own.
  • How would you detect this class pre-release? → Test BOOT_COMPLETED on a low-end device in the lab, plus a CI check that measures receivers with StrictMode.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team lost two days optimizing a screen render path because a Slack screenshot of a logcat warning was treated as evidence; a 10-minute ANR-type breakdown in the vitals console pointed to a broadcast receiver instead.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: chases startup optimization, blames the engineer.
  • Hire: classifies ANR types, finds receiver main-thread work, moves to WorkManager.
  • Strong hire: identifies the red herring and triage failure, gives a runbook, repro via am broadcast/reboot, release gating and blameless process improvements.
